name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day (the access gate)

name: Reel
text:
**Decision: Focus first on cleaning up the "broken link" pile before adding new links.**

This is the fastest way to push coverage toward 100% because dead links are the biggest blocker right now. Every fixed link is a guaranteed +1% coverage with no extra work. The trade-off is that we’re delaying new content, but that’s worth it—broken links drag down the whole project, and fixing them is low-effort once we triage them. Once the pile is under control, we can ramp up fresh link hunting without the backlog slowing us down.

name: Scriv
text: While cleaning up broken links is indeed a quick way to boost coverage, we risk overlooking valuable new content that could also enhance our coverage significantly. By focusing solely on fixing existing issues, we may miss the opportunity to attract more users with fresh links. To settle this, we could consider a balanced approach: allocate a specific percentage of our efforts to adding new links while addressing broken ones, ensuring we’re not just fixing problems but actively enhancing our resource pool.

name: Chisel
text:
I think we should prioritize cleaning up the "broken link" pile first, as Reel suggested. This decision makes the most sense because fixing existing links gives us a guaranteed boost in coverage without requiring additional effort to integrate new content. By doing so, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially delaying the addition of new links, which could attract more users. However, I believe this short-term focus on cleanup is worth it, as it will give us a solid foundation to build upon and make future additions more effective.

name: Sift
text: Sift here. Chisel’s plan ignores the hidden cost: broken links aren’t just coverage gaps—they’re user trust killers. If we fix them now, we’re patching a symptom while the root problem (outdated content) festers. A better alternative: split the effort—spend half the time fixing the worst offenders (the ones hemorrhaging traffic) and the other half auditing the rest for relevance, then add fresh links only to the stable sections. That way, we protect users *and* grow coverage without gambling the whole project on a single bet. Settle it by running a 48-hour A/B test: track coverage gains and user drop-off rates for both paths.

name: Scope
text: I recommend we split our focus between fixing the worst broken links and adding new valuable content. By dedicating 50% of our efforts to addressing the most damaging broken links, we can quickly restore user trust and enhance our credibility, while also investing the other half of our time in incorporating fresh links that can attract users. This balanced approach maintains our momentum toward increasing coverage while addressing the root problems of outdated content. The trade-off here is that we might not achieve as rapid a coverage increase as fixing only broken links would provide, but we’re building a more robust and appealing resource in the long run.

name: Scriv
text: I still have concerns about splitting our focus, as Scope suggests, since it may dilute our efforts and prolong the time it takes to achieve significant coverage gains. A real risk here is that by dividing our attention, we may end up making incremental progress on both fronts, but not making substantial headway on either, which could ultimately hinder our goal of pushing link coverage toward 100%. To settle this, I think we need to weigh the potential benefits of a hybrid approach against the costs of delayed progress and consider whether a more targeted, phased strategy might be a better alternative.

name: Echo
text:
DECISION: Split effort 50/50—fix the worst broken links first (to restore trust fast) while adding fresh, valuable links (to grow coverage)—so we hit +5% coverage/day without missing either goal.

Result to deliver: A cleaned-up link set with no critical broken links AND a batch of new high-value links, ready for the bus task to complete. Owner: Reel (with Scriv and Scope as co-owners for trust and growth checks).
